verdict: Thirty-six answers with real substance and some passages only James could have written, wearing a machine's habits: 56 em-dashes in the first fifteen answers, an epigram closing about thirty of the thirty-six, deny-then-assert antithesis as the default sentence, the editorial rulebook's vocabulary in the last twelve, and essay images left stranded by compression. All 101 findings carry an exact replacement; none changes a fact, quotation or reference.
note: quote and replacement are raw source text of the TypeScript file (\" is an escaped quotation mark). Each quote occurs exactly once. Apply in order; no two quotes overlap.

patterns.pattern: Em-dashes (56, all in the first fifteen answers)
patterns.note: Lines 32 to 202 only. The later twenty-one answers have none, so the library reads as two different drafts. Every one of the 56 has a replacement in the JSON. scripts/validate-no-emdash.mjs does not scan client/src/data/answers.ts, which is how they survived.

patterns.pattern: Aphoristic two-beat closers (about thirty of thirty-six answers end on one)
patterns.note: The single biggest tell. Each answer's last line is an epigram, usually a matched pair. Two answers close on the same mould ('not asking to be trusted blindly... asking to be opened' / 'did not ask to be believed blindly... asked to be weighed'). The ones worth keeping because the answer earned them: 'I just don't think it can hold you', 'The crutch was real. It was just in my other hand', 'The floor held anyway. It is worth asking who laid it', 'It would not stay closed', 'He entered it'.

patterns.pattern: 'It is not X. It is Y.' as the default gait (27 two-sentence instances, 15 'was never')
patterns.note: Worst in is-jesus-the-only-way (seven in one answer), are-miracles-believable, should-a-christian-follow-a-political-party and can-life-mean-anything-without-god (the same antithesis three times).

patterns.pattern: Rulebook leakage (the editorial method written into the prose)
patterns.note: 'second-order', 'first-order', 'third-order', 'confessional floor', 'confessional core', 'at full strength', 'at their strongest', 'full due', 'Grant', 'Concede', 'Refuse both cheap versions', 'remain a brother', 'verdict', 'indictment'. Readers do not sort doctrine into orders; the rulebook does. Concentrated in the last twelve answers.

patterns.pattern: Compressions that no longer parse without the essay
patterns.note: Images and referents carried over from the full essay with their setup cut: the dark kitchen and glass of water, 'that accusation', the ocean (Trinity), the wall (anxiety), 'the running' (teenager), 'the specific child', 'closes the fawn'.

patterns.pattern: Stamps and motifs repeated across answers
patterns.note: 'honest/honestly' 13 times as a self-certifying word; the moral 'floor' eight times in six answers; 'None of this/that' opening a sentence in four answers; 'no friend of / no apologist' three times; 'the whole time' three times; the paragraph-three confession ('I once thought', 'I used to play this', 'I ran the projection test', 'I say this against myself', 'I held the comfortable view', 'I made the math objection for years') in roughly twenty answers. See also the floor fix under can-life-mean-anything-without-god and the 'None of' fixes under what-about-those-who-never-heard and why-does-god-allow-natural-disasters.
Also the symmetry findings: 'Objective, because... Not arbitrary, because...' and 'Biblical faith is reaching for reasons the whole time. Reason is running on trust the whole time.'

strengths: is-faith-just-wishful-thinking (the fatherless boy and the Godless sky; nobody else could write that paragraph)
can-you-be-a-christian-without-church (for 'You can hold the faith by yourself. I just don't think it can hold you.')
for_james: Biography to confirm, because I could not check it and would not invent around it: 'I built an atheism at nineteen' (what-happens-after-deconstruction); 'For most of my life I was an atheist' and 'a man who spent most of his life certain no one was there' (is-jesus-the-only-way, does-god-actually-exist); 'They were right about the church I was leaving' (what-did-the-new-atheists-get-right), which implies you were inside a church before you believed; 'on a night when I was the thing that had broken' (can-life-mean-anything-without-god); 'I have watched the anger last into the tenth year' (is-it-okay-to-be-angry-at-god); 'You are describing my inbox' (is-faith-just-wishful-thinking). If any of these is not literally true, tell us and we cut it.

Your atheist past appears in about twenty of the thirty-six answers, nearly always opening the third paragraph. Each one is fine alone; together it becomes a formula and starts working as a credential. Pick the eight or ten answers where it is doing real work (wishful thinking, slavery, genocide, does God exist, good without God are the strongest) and let us plain-state the rest.

should-a-christian-follow-a-political-party: the right gets a date and a mechanism ('After 1979 a voter guide functioned as a catechism'); the left gets only a metaphor ('the same lie in a different accent'). The essay presumably names the left's version as concretely. Give us the one sentence you would use so the instrument is the same in both directions.

The two anxiety answers pull against each other. what-does-the-bible-say-about-anxiety calls worry 'a quiet declaration that he is not there' and 'a practical atheism'; is-anxiety-a-spiritual-failure says 'Anxiety is not a verdict on your faith, and the person who told you it was did you real harm.' A reader with an anxiety disorder who lands on the first one gets no help line and something close to the pietist answer the second one rejects. Decide whether the first should say it is about ordinary worry, and point to the second.

Path to help: the answers are plain strings and Answers.tsx renders no Find Help link, so the divorce answer ('If you are in danger, get safe first') and the natural-evil answer ('If you are in the middle of this') name no next step. Only the anxiety answer carries 988. Simplest fix is a Find Help link under those answers in the page; that is an engineering change, not a wording change.

Facts to verify against the essays (I changed none of them): 'Jesus spoke about money and possessions more than he spoke about heaven and hell combined' (a popular claim that is hard to source); Kepler 'thinking God's thoughts after him' (widely attributed, hard to find verbatim); the Nagel quotation's punctuation; 'a desperate father with a dying child' for Mark 9, where the boy is tormented, not said to be dying; Holland and Hurtado appear by surname only, with no first name or idea-label for a reader who has not met them.

Mark 9:24 is quoted three times, twice without its exclamation point and once with it. The ESV has 'I believe; help my unbelief!'. '(…, ESV)' is appended to four references and not the rest. Psalm 13:1, Psalm 22:1 and John 6:68 are quoted without quotation marks. Tell us which convention you want and we will make all thirty-six match.

Where your saved Substack profile and VOICE-JAMES-BELL.md disagree, I followed VOICE-JAMES-BELL.md as instructed. The profile asks for 'stacked landing lines', a screenshot line in every piece, and two-to-four-sentence paragraphs; the voice standard asks for developed paragraphs and one earned verdict. These answers were written toward the profile, which is where most of the pillow closers come from.

Contractions: the library has almost none ('I just don't think it can hold you' is the rare one, and it is the best line in the file). The replacements use them lightly. If you want the answers fully uncontracted, say so.

The file's own header says each answer is 'three tight paragraphs'. The first fifteen average about 75 words a paragraph; the last twenty-one run 150 to 250. That is two drafts by two hands and a reader can feel the seam. Worth deciding which length you want.
